title: Big-spending AI resist creators
full_text:
AI giants are spending billions of dollars on the infrastructure to develop their models but not on the information used to train them, says an executive who built one of Australia’s biggest media intelligence companies.
The federal government has been accused of a secret copyright “betrayal” after leaked confidential documents revealed it was considering copyright changes that risk compromising creatives’ intellectual property.
The government has previously pledged that it will protect Australian creatives and other copyright holders as AI behemoths push to water down laws to train the models.
OpenAI has declared that it will not even consider investing in domestic AI training or renewable energy if the government refuses to weaken copyright protection.
But John Croll, who founded international media outfit Truescope, after previously leading local powerhouse iSentia, can’t understand why OpenAI, Claude maker Anthropic and other AI companies cannot strike licensing deals with media outlets and creators as he has done.
“The hyperscalers are spending billions on the infrastructure to develop their service, but they seem unwilling to spend millions on the information that actually delivers the service, which is information to the end user,” he said.
“These companies speak of the scale in which they operate; with the tools at their disposal they can provide a licensing regime that covers the data and information they use.
“Companies like Truescope have been licensing with content owners and collecting societies for years. If we can do it, there is no doubt they can do it.” Senate crossbencher David Pocock has revealed confidential documents with options on copyright changes that he said showed the federal government could compromise on creatives’ intellectual property despite promising to do otherwise.
The documents show two policies apparently being considered on how to change copyright law in the face of the AI boom.
Both options include an opt out – which would mean that “any rights holders who do not want to have online material trained can opt out by adopting digital protection to stop AI from crawling and training on content”.
Mr Croll, who delayed the local launch of Truescope until it secured licensing deals, said the government had only “one chance to get this right”.
“Once indexed in the large-language models, it is a valuable source of information for the hyperscalers to sell forever,” he said.
Copyright has become a flashpoint beyond Australia.
Sony Group and Warner Music are suing Anthropic in California over its alleged theft of copyrighted songs to train its models.
Facebook owner Meta is facing similar allegations in New York after five publishers accused founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg of personally ordering the pirating of millions of books rather than paying for them.
The federal Coalition has accused the government of considering policy options it had explicitly ruled out and of “the hallmarks of a dirty deal to hand the intellectual property of Australian creators to global AI giants”.
Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton has said that the AI and data-centre revolution would rival the mining boom’s economic output from 2003 to 2013, but provide more long-lasting benefits through productivity gains.
Meanwhile, Atlassian billionaire and Tech Council of Australia chair Scott Farquhar has said local AI training could unlock a multibillion-dollar opportunity for the nation.
There was $8.7bn of investment in data centres in the March quarter, accounting for 17 per cent of all private sector spending.
Treasury predicts AI will add $116bn to GDP over the next decade, an estimate Dr Charlton regarded as “cautious”.
The government’s optimism comes amid warnings about AI’s threat to humanity. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned last week, said the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade” and AI labs were “gambling with our lives”.
OpenAI chief Sam Altman acknowledged the public’s fear that competition between companies and countries might sideline safety and backed support for industry collaboration to develop a new standards body.
“I think it’s great for our industry to say we want to come together and we want to be able to co-ordinate and make sure we have enough time to do this safely,” he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference in San Francisco. “When there’s any implication …” that some in the industry might “not do the right thing, I think that’s when people get very scared”.
